title: Structured Approach
body:
Decompose the system by **function**. Start with what it has to do, break that into
sub-functions, break those down again, and keep going until each piece is small enough to
write. The classic tools are the structure chart and the data flow diagram, and the classic
result is a tree of procedures with the data they operate on held separately, which is how a
C program is usually organised.

Its weakness is where the data lives. Because functions and data are separate, a change to a
data structure reaches every function that touches it, and there is nothing in the design
that limits how many that is. The [[Object Oriented Approach]] is the answer to exactly that:
keep the data and the operations on it in one place ([[Encapsulation]]) so the blast radius
of a change is the object.

| | Structured | [[Object Oriented Approach|Object oriented]] |
|---|---|---|
| Decomposes by | function | thing |
| Data and behaviour | separate | together |
| Unit of reuse | the procedure | the class |
| Change to a data structure | touches every user of it | contained by the class |
| Fits | pipelines, transforms, small systems | domains with stable nouns |

Neither is obsolete. Structured decomposition is still how you design a single function, and
[[Abstraction]] and [[Coupling and Cohesion]] are the goals under both approaches; they
disagree only about what the modules are.

See [[Paradigms]] and [[Design]].
